name: Raloxifene (Evista)

lead: Raloxifene is a prescription SERM approved for osteoporosis and breast cancer risk reduction in postmenopausal women. Men use it off-label to shrink gynecomastia tissue and flatten the chest, including puberty-onset cases, often alongside or after tamoxifen.

It blocks estrogen action in breast tissue and mimics it in bone. Forum posters report shrinkage and some regrowth after stopping. Published evidence for this use is limited to small studies, such as a retrospective review in adolescent boys.

paras: It is a daily oral tablet taken for months. Users describe gradual shrinkage and often continue until results plateau.

The label carries a boxed warning for blood clots and stroke death; common effects include hot flashes, leg cramps and swelling. It is prescription-only, contraindicated in pregnancy, and not approved for men.

angle.text: Raloxifene is a SERM that men use off-label to shrink gynecomastia: it blocks estrogen action in breast tissue, which reduces gland tissue and flattens the chest. Forum posters report shrinkage and regrowth after stopping, and published evidence is limited to small studies.

lead: Raloxifene (brand name Evista) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) approved in the US for treating and preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and for reducing the risk of invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or at high risk.[1][2] It acts as an estrogen agonist in bone and an antagonist in breast and uterine tissue.[2][3]

For appearance, it is discussed in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities as an off-label oral option for gynecomastia, the benign enlargement of male breast tissue, with the aim of a flatter, more defined chest. Users describe it as an alternative or follow-up to tamoxifen, with surgery as the other route.[4][5][6] Published evidence for that use consists of a small retrospective chart review in adolescent boys; it is not an approved indication.[1][3]

Raloxifene was approved in 1997 and has a large research base in women, including the MORE and STAR trials.[7][8][9] That research concerns bone and breast-cancer outcomes in postmenopausal women rather than gynecomastia in men.
infobox: Benzothiophene derivative; unlike triphenylethylene SERMs such as tamoxifen[1]

paras: Raloxifene is used for postmenopausal osteoporosis, though bisphosphonates are generally preferred, and for reducing breast cancer risk in high-risk postmenopausal women.[1] It is not indicated for treating invasive breast cancer or reducing recurrence.[2] It does not relieve hot flashes and may worsen them.[3] An early trial examined its effects on bone mineral density, cholesterol and the uterine lining in postmenopausal women.[10] Because it acts as an anti-estrogen in the breast but does not stimulate the uterus the way tamoxifen does, it became the main alternative to tamoxifen for chemoprevention in postmenopausal women.[1][9]

Gynecomastia affects an estimated 35 percent of men over a lifetime, and up to 70 percent of adolescent boys show some degree of it, with about three-quarters of those cases resolving within two years without treatment.[6] It stems from an altered estrogen-to-androgen balance, and causes include puberty, ageing, medications, and endocrine or liver conditions.[6] Wikipedia's gynecomastia article lists tamoxifen and raloxifene as SERMs that may help but are not FDA-approved for it, and describes surgery as the usual route when tissue is long-standing and fibrotic.[6]
On looksmax.org, posters describe raloxifene as a second-line drug after or alongside tamoxifen, ask whether tissue returns after stopping, and weigh the drug against surgery.[4][5]

A small retrospective chart review reported that raloxifene was effective for pubertal gynecomastia in adolescent boys; Wikipedia notes other SERMs also treat gynecomastia.[1] Grokipedia, citing that kind of data, describes a greater than 50 percent reduction in breast tissue volume in most of the treated boys, but this is a small off-label dataset.[3] Wikipedia's gynecomastia article describes tamoxifen as the best-supported medical option, clomifene as less effective, and aromatase inhibitors as less effective than SERMs.[6]

In men, raloxifene is reported to raise testosterone through effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, although free testosterone often stays unchanged.[1] Men have also been studied with it in schizophrenia, prostate cancer and osteoporosis research.[1] Looksmax.org posters describe using raloxifene after or alongside tamoxifen for gynecomastia and ask whether it returns after stopping; other posters argue surgery is preferable and ask about side effects.[4][5]

Common effects are hot flashes, leg cramps, peripheral edema, flu syndrome, joint pain and sweating.[2] In trials, hot flashes were reported by 25 to 28 percent of raloxifene users versus 18 to 21 percent on placebo, and leg cramps by 5.5 versus 1.9 percent.[1] The label carries a boxed warning for increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism and for increased risk of death from stroke in women with coronary heart disease or elevated risk; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in people with a history of venous thromboembolism.[2] Venous thromboembolism risk is roughly three times higher on treatment.[1] Unlike tamoxifen it does not increase uterine hyperplasia or endometrial cancer risk, and it does not appear to cause breast pain or affect cognition.[1][11] The label data come from postmenopausal women, so male-specific safety rests on small studies.

Raloxifene binds estrogen receptors and its agonist or antagonist action depends on recruitment of coactivators and corepressors to target gene promoters in each tissue.[2][12] It is a partial agonist at estrogen receptor alpha, an antagonist at beta, and an agonist at the G protein-coupled estrogen receptor.[1] Structural work in 1997 described the molecular basis of agonism and antagonism at the estrogen receptor.[13] Effects include lower LDL cholesterol, reduced breast density and increased bone density in postmenopausal women.[1]

Oral bioavailability is about 2 percent owing to first-pass metabolism, though absorption is about 60 percent; it is metabolised by glucuronidation and has a half-life of roughly 28 to 33 hours.[1] It is chemically a benzothiophene and the only marketed SERM of that class.[1]

Raloxifene, developed under names such as keoxifene and LY-139481, was approved in the US in 1997 for preventing postmenopausal osteoporosis and in 1999 for treating it.[1] It received orphan drug designation in 2005 and approval for breast cancer risk reduction in 2007, when a boxed warning on stroke death was also added.[1] Generic versions are widely sold.[1] Its use for gynecomastia developed in clinical case series and then in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums, which discuss it as an alternative to tamoxifen.[4][5]

In the MORE trial of 7,705 postmenopausal women, raloxifene reduced the risk of new vertebral fractures by about 30 percent [7][14] and reduced breast cancer incidence, including a 72 percent reduction in invasive breast cancer according to Wikipedia's summary.[8][1] The STAR trial compared raloxifene with tamoxifen in high-risk postmenopausal women and found similar invasive-breast-cancer prevention with a lower thromboembolism risk.[1][9] The RUTH trial examined cardiovascular events and breast cancer, and a cognition sub-study ran alongside STAR in 1,498 women.[15][11]

Smaller registered trials have tested raloxifene in schizophrenia, Alzheimer's disease and endometriosis.[16][17] No controlled trial in men with gynecomastia was identified; the evidence is the small retrospective review described above.[1]
